title: The Sharpe Pint

opening_mood.text: Happy Saturday. Grab a coffee, shake off the week, and let's get you properly set up for the weekend. We have had a wild week in the City: geopolitical oil shocks dictating central bank policy in Frankfurt, a massive sigh of relief on US inflation, and an AI hardware party triggered by Oracle that shows the physical infrastructure layer is still printing money. Whether you are prepping for interviews, trying to sound smart in front of your VP, or just looking for some high-quality ammunition for your next pub debate, we have got you covered. Let's dive in.

content.text: It has been a busy 24 hours across the City and Wall Street. From central bank surprises to massive tech consolidation, here are the five stories that actually matter for your commercial awareness.
1. ECB Hikes to 2.5% as Strait of Hormuz Flare-up Sends Oil Past $105

The European Central Bank (ECB) raised its key deposit rate by 25 basis points to 2.5% (and the main refinancing rate to 2.65%). ECB President Christine Lagarde called the unanimous decision a "no-brainer" after preliminary Eurozone inflation jumped to 3.3% in August, driven by a massive spike in energy costs. The spike followed US and Iranian military clashes in the Strait of Hormuz, which briefly pushed Brent crude past $105 a barrel earlier in the week.

Geopolitics is directly dictating monetary policy again. The ECB was forced to revise its 2027 and 2028 inflation forecasts upward (to 2.5% and 2.1% respectively), admitting that price pressures will be "longer lasting" than previously hoped. On the bright side, they upgraded their 2026 growth forecast to 0.9% due to economic resilience. This hawkish tone sent European bond yields soaring, with UK 10-year gilt yields hitting a 19-year high, setting a very tense stage for the Federal Reserve and the Bank of England next week.

items: What to say at work: Lagarde's 'no-brainer' comment shows that central banks are terrified of second-round effects from this Middle East energy shock. Even though the Bank of England is widely expected to hold at 3.75% next week, gilt yields hitting a 19-year high show the market is pricing in a much more painful, higher-for-longer path.

Interview tip: If asked about the transmission mechanism of geopolitical risk to monetary policy, use this week as a textbook example. A supply-side shock in the Strait of Hormuz immediately spikes Brent crude, which feeds into headline CPI, forcing central banks to hike rates to prevent those energy costs from de-anchoring long-term inflation expectations.

content.text: 2. US Core Inflation Cools to 2.4%, Giving the Fed Some Breathing Room

US stocks broke a brutal four-day losing streak on Friday after the August CPI report came in exactly as the market hoped. Headline inflation held steady at 3.4% year-on-year (up 0.4% month-on-month, driven by a 3.9% jump in gasoline prices). However, core CPI (excluding volatile food and energy) slowed to 2.4% year-on-year—the lowest reading since March 2021.

While the geopolitical oil spike is keeping headline inflation sticky, the cooling of core inflation to 2.4% suggests that underlying domestic price pressures are still moderating. This gives the Federal Reserve the green light to proceed with a standard 25bps cut or hold next week, rather than having to panic-react to the energy shock. Markets hate uncertainty, and this "as expected" print triggered a massive sigh of relief.

items: What to say at work: The August CPI is a classic 'no news is good news' print. The headline 3.4% looks ugly because of the energy spike, but the core dropping to 2.4% is what the Fed actually cares about. It shows the underlying disinflationary trend is intact, keeping a measured rate path on the table.

The City Angle: This print prevents a worst-case scenario where the Fed would feel forced to pause or even hike in the face of stagflationary energy pressures. Fixed income desks are breathing a massive sigh of relief.

content.text: 3. Dell and HPE Hit Record Highs as Oracle Validates the AI Capex Boom

Shares of server and networking giants Dell Technologies and Hewlett Packard Enterprise (HPE) led the S&P 500 on Friday, surging 12% and 12.4% respectively to hit all-time closing highs. The catalyst was Oracle's blockbuster Q1 earnings, which revealed a massive $664 billion in remaining performance obligations (including $30 billion in new AI cloud contracts) and an aggressive capital expenditure plan.

Oracle's numbers prove that the AI infrastructure buildout is translating into hard, massive capital spending that directly flows to hardware suppliers. HPE also benefited from its newly expanded partnership with Oracle to deploy HPE's routing and switching platforms across Oracle's global data centres. Meanwhile, RBC Capital initiated coverage on Dell with a bullish "Outperform" rating and a $640 price target, highlighting Dell's $95 billion AI server backlog.

items: What to say at work: Oracle's capex guidance is the ultimate rising tide for hardware. Dell and HPE surging to record highs shows that the market is rotating away from pure-play chipmakers like Nvidia and into the systems and networking integrators who actually build and connect the data centres.

The Quant/AI Angle: For asset managers, the trade is shifting from 'who makes the chips' to 'who has the power, cooling, and networking gear to actually run them.' HPE's partnership with Oracle on routing and switching is a prime example of networking becoming the ultimate bottleneck in LLM training.

content.text: 4. Copart Drops $1.9bn in Cash to Buy ACV Auctions and Dominate Wholesale

Online vehicle auction giant Copart (CPRT) announced a definitive agreement to acquire digital automotive marketplace ACV Auctions (ACVA) for $10.50 per share in cash, valuing the company at approximately $1.9 billion. Following the announcement, ACV shares surged over 44% to trade close to the offer price.

Copart's core business has traditionally been online auctions for salvage and total-loss vehicles (working closely with insurance companies). By buying ACV, Copart is aggressively expanding into the adjacent, highly lucrative dealer-to-dealer wholesale used vehicle marketplace. ACV brings advanced digital inspection data and AI-powered valuation tools (like ClearCar and VIPER), which Copart can scale across its massive global footprint.

items: What to say at work: Copart's acquisition of ACV Auctions is a textbook vertical expansion. Copart is dominant in salvage, but by buying ACV for $1.9bn, they instantly capture the dealer-to-dealer wholesale market and acquire proprietary AI valuation tech.

M&A discussion point: The 45% premium over ACV's unaffected price shows how much value Copart places on ACV's digital data and AI tools. In a mature industry like auto remarketing, buying the tech is often faster and cheaper than trying to build a digital marketplace from scratch.

content.text: 5. Bain-Backed Envestnet Buys Vestmark to Create a $10 Trillion WealthTech Giant

Envestnet, a leading wealth technology platform backed by Bain Capital, announced a definitive agreement to acquire Vestmark, a premier provider of portfolio management and trading technology. Vestmark supports over $2 trillion in assets and 5 million investor accounts. Financial terms of the deal were not disclosed, but it is expected to close in Q4 2026.

Envestnet already serves more than a third of all US financial advisors and manages approximately $8 trillion in platform assets. By absorbing Vestmark, Envestnet is significantly upgrading its direct indexing, tax transition management, and portfolio rebalancing capabilities. Private equity is continuing to drive massive consolidation in the wealth management and asset management technology stack.

items: What to say at work: The Envestnet-Vestmark deal is a classic private equity roll-up play by Bain Capital. WealthTech is highly fragmented, but by combining Envestnet's $8 trillion platform with Vestmark's $2 trillion portfolio management tech, they are creating an absolute behemoth.

Asset Management Angle: Direct indexing and personalised tax management are growing rapidly as high-net-worth clients demand more than just generic ETFs. This acquisition gives Envestnet the institutional-grade engine to deliver that customisation at massive scale.

sections.title: Markets Briefing: What Moved and Why

content.text: It was a classic case of "bad news is digested, but at least it's not worse" in the Friday session. After a bruising four-day losing streak, the S&P 500 snapped back, gaining 0.86% to close at 7,656.98, while the Nasdaq Composite climbed 0.96% to 26,333. The catalyst? A highly anticipated August CPI print that landed almost exactly on the nose of expectations, giving a bruised market just enough breathing room to stage a Friday afternoon bounce.
The Warsh Fed Faces Its First Real Test

Let’s look under the hood. Headline inflation held steady at 3.4% year-on-year, but core CPI came in a touch warmer at 0.3% month-on-month. In normal times, a warm core print might have triggered a fresh tantrum. But with the market already pricing in a hawkish shift, this print essentially cemented what everyone was whispering: a Fed rate hike next week is now a near-certainty. CME FedWatch pricing for a 25-basis-point hike next week (which would take the target range to 3.75%–4.00%) shot up to nearly 90%, up from a coin-flip just a few weeks ago. This will be the first major policy test for Kevin Warsh since he took the big chair in May, and his preference for "intentional ambiguity" and pulling back on forward guidance means next week's FOMC meeting is going to be a proper live event.
The Cross-Asset Read: Oil, Yields, and Central Bank Co-ordination
Why did equities rally if a rate hike is locked in? It’s all about the cross-asset relief:

items: The Oil Pressure Valve: Brent crude, which had spiked to a painful $108 a barrel on Thursday as the conflict with Iran threatened the Strait of Hormuz, pulled back nearly 3% on Friday to settle around $105. That took some immediate heat off the inflation panic.

Treasury Yields Pause: Bond yields have been on a tear, with the 2-year Treasury hitting 4.60% and the 10-year touching 4.95% earlier in the week. Friday saw a mild retreat from these multi-decade highs, which acted as a green light for equity buyers to step back in.

Global Central Bank Sync: It’s not just a US story. The European Central Bank delivered a 25bps "insurance hike" to 2.50% earlier in the week to buffer against the energy shock, and the Bank of Japan is widely expected to follow suit on September 18. The market is realising that global central banks are moving in lockstep to build a defensive wall against this latest oil shock.

content.text: AI Capex is Still the Ultimate Shield

If you want to know where the real money went on Friday, look at AI infrastructure. Oracle’s blockbuster earnings and eye-watering data centre capex plans earlier in the week acted as a massive reassurance policy. It proved that whatever the macro headwinds, the tech giants are still spending heavily on AI hardware. Hewlett Packard Enterprise (HPE) surged 12.44% to $62.09, Dell Technologies jumped 11.98% to $567.30, and Arista Networks gained 5.61% to $199.59. When the macro gets tough, the market hides in secular growth stories with guaranteed demand.
Over the Pint: What to Say at the Pub

If you’re chatting with colleagues or clients, the talking point is clear: the "Powell Put" is dead, and we are firmly in the "Warsh Regime". Warsh wants the market to do the tightening for him by letting yields run, but with core inflation sticky and oil hovering over $100, he’s being forced to act. The fact that equities rallied on a 90% chance of a rate hike shows that the market has finally accepted that higher-for-longer isn't just a threat—it's the baseline. If you're interviewing, watch how the yield curve reacts next week; a hawkish hike that flattens the curve further suggests the market thinks the Fed might oversteer into a slowdown.

sections.title: Financial Idea of the Day: The Make-Whole Call

content.text: The Make-Whole Call: The Bond Market's Golden Handcuffs

Imagine you have locked in a beautiful 6% yield on a corporate bond, only for market interest rates to plummet to 3%. You are feeling like a financial genius, smugly sipping your pint, until you remember the issuer has a call option to buy back the bond early. If this were a traditional call option, the company could snatch your high-yielding bond away at a fixed price—say, 103% of par—leaving you to reinvest your cash in a miserable low-yield market. But if your bond has a Make-Whole Call (MWC) provision, the tables are turned. The issuer can still take the bond back, but they have to pay you a price that genuinely makes you whole for the interest you are losing.
How the Mechanics Actually Work

Unlike a traditional call option with a fixed price (e.g., 103 or 101), a make-whole call price is dynamic. It is calculated as the net present value (NPV) of all the remaining coupon and principal payments you would have received if the bond had run to maturity. To calculate this NPV, the bond's indenture specifies a discount rate equal to a benchmark government bond yield (like a US Treasury or a UK Gilt of similar maturity) plus a tiny, predetermined spread—typically between 15 and 50 basis points (0.15% to 0.50%).

Let's look at a quick example. Suppose a company wants to redeem a bond with a 6.0% coupon and 5 years left to maturity. If the comparable 5-year Gilt yield is currently 3.0%, and the make-whole spread in the bond's contract is 25 bps, the discount rate used for the NPV calculation is 3.25% (3.0% + 0.25%). Because we are discounting a 6.0% stream of cash flows at a much lower rate of 3.25%, the resulting present value is going to be massive—roughly £112.60 per £100 of face value. The issuer has to pay you this premium price, effectively handing you your future interest up front, discounted at a very low rate.
Why It Matters in the City

items: For Asset Managers: MWCs are a godsend. They eliminate the severe reinvestment risk that plagues traditional callable bonds. If an issuer exercises an MWC, the investor is fully compensated for the lost yield, meaning the bond behaves almost like a non-callable bullet bond for valuation and duration purposes.

For Corporate Issuers & Debt Capital Markets (DCM): Why would an issuer agree to this? Flexibility. If a company is being acquired, wants to break free of restrictive covenants, or needs to restructure its balance sheet, it might need to retire its debt immediately. The MWC gives them the legal right to do so at any time, even if the financial penalty is eye-watering.

The Par-Call Window: Because MWCs are so expensive, almost all investment-grade corporate bonds combine them with a par-call window in the final 3 to 6 months before maturity. This allows the corporate treasury team to refinance the debt at par (100) just before it matures without paying the punitive make-whole premium.

content.text: The Classic Interview Trap

In an investment banking or credit research interview, a classic question is: 'If interest rates fall, which bond price will rise more: a bond with a traditional call option, or a bond with a make-whole call option?'

The answer is the bond with the make-whole call. A traditional callable bond suffers from price compression (or negative convexity) as rates fall, because its price is capped near the fixed call price (e.g., 103). Nobody will pay 110 for a bond that the company can buy back tomorrow for 103. However, because the make-whole call price rises as interest rates fall (since the discount rate decreases), the bond's price can rise freely, tracking the value of a non-callable bond.
Pub Talk: How to Sound Smart

"If we are looking to acquire Target Co and clean up their capital structure, we need to look closely at their outstanding debt. If those bonds have make-whole provisions and were locked in when yields were high, refinancing them early is going to cost us an absolute fortune. We might be better off leaving them on the balance sheet or waiting for the par-call window."

sections.title: Quant / AI Finance Idea of the Day: Asymptotically-Informed Neural Networks

content.text: The Concept: Asymptotically-Informed Neural Networks (AINNs)

When it comes to options trading, speed is life. If you are calibrating a complex volatility surface or running a high-frequency market-making book, you need to invert the Black-Scholes formula to find implied volatility (IV) millions of times a second. Traditional numerical solvers (like Brent's method) are too slow, while standard deep learning surrogates—though fast—miserably fail in the 'asymptotic regimes' (deep out-of-the-money, extreme strikes, or ultra-short maturities) where the inverse mapping becomes hyper-sensitive to tiny perturbations.

Enter Asymptotically-Informed Neural Networks (AINNs). Instead of treating IV inversion as a generic regression problem, AINNs embed the analytical structure of the Black-Scholes formula directly into the network architecture. The model acts as a specialised Mixture-of-Experts (MoE): it uses a trainable gating network to partition the price-log-moneyness domain into distinct regimes (low-volatility, high-volatility, and central) and combines specialised local neural approximations for each region. The result is blazing-fast inference with accuracy that is orders of magnitude better than standard neural nets, especially in the extreme tails.
How It Works: A Hybrid Approach

The magic doesn't stop at the neural network. Because the AINN's prediction is so close to the true value, it provides an exceptionally high-quality initial guess. Quants can then run a high-order numerical refiner—specifically a third-order Householder scheme—to polish the guess to machine precision. Because the starting point is so accurate, the solver converges in just one or two iterations, completely bypassing the slow search phases of traditional solvers.
Python-Style Implementation

import numpy as np

class AsymptoticallyInformedIVModel:
    def __init__(self, low_vol_expert, high_vol_expert, central_expert):
        self.low_vol_expert = low_vol_expert
        self.high_vol_expert = high_vol_expert
        self.central_expert = central_expert
        
    def gating_network(self, price, log_moneyness):
        # In practice, this is a trainable neural network or analytical boundary
        # Let's simulate gating weights (probabilities) summing to 1
        w_low = np.exp(-price * 5)  # High weight when price is near lower bound
        w_high = np.exp(-(1 - price) * 5) # High weight when price is near upper bound
        w_central = 1.0 - (w_low + w_high)
        
        # Normalize
        total = w_low + w_high + w_central
        return w_low/total, w_high/total, w_central/total

    def predict_initial_guess(self, price, log_moneyness):
        w_low, w_high, w_central = self.gating_network(price, log_moneyness)
        
        # Get predictions from specialized local experts
        sigma_low = self.low_vol_expert(price, log_moneyness)
        sigma_high = self.high_vol_expert(price, log_moneyness)
        sigma_central = self.central_expert(price, log_moneyness)
        
        # Mixture of experts output
        return w_low * sigma_low + w_high * sigma_high + w_central * sigma_central

def householder_refinement_3rd_order(initial_guess, target_price, bs_pricing_func, max_iter=2):
    """
    Polishes the neural network's initial guess to machine precision
    using a 3rd-order Householder root-finding scheme.
    """
    sigma = initial_guess
    for _ in range(max_iter):
        # Compute Black-Scholes price and its derivatives (Vega, Volga, etc.)
        price, vega, volga = bs_pricing_func(sigma)
        f = price - target_price
        
        # Householder 3rd-order update formula
        h = -f / vega
        ratio = volga / vega
        update = h * (1.0 + 0.5 * h * ratio)
        sigma += update
    return sigma
The Paper Angle

This approach is detailed in the paper, 'Asymptotically-informed neural networks for Black-Scholes implied volatility computation' (August 2026) by Samira Amiriyan and Youness Boutaib from the University of Liverpool. The authors demonstrate that by incorporating analytical knowledge of the Black-Scholes formula's asymptotic limits, they can train smaller, more robust networks that generalise beautifully and avoid the 'black-box' failures of standard deep learning in extreme market conditions.
The Interview & Pub Conversation Starter

items: In an interview: If asked how to accelerate option pricing or model calibration using ML, don't just say 'train a neural net.' That's a rookie answer that ignores boundary failures. Instead, explain how you would use an AINN: 'I'd partition the domain into asymptotic regimes using analytical boundaries, train specialised local networks for each regime, glue them together with a gating network, and then polish the output to machine precision using a fast Householder scheme.' This shows you understand both modern ML and classical quantitative finance.

Over a pint: 'Everyone is trying to build LLMs for finance, but the real money is still in the plumbing. Standard neural nets are blind to the mathematical boundaries of options pricing. AINNs are basically a Mixture-of-Experts where the gating is dictated by the actual physics of the Black-Scholes formula. It's the ultimate hybrid of machine learning speed and classical mathematical rigour.'

content.text: The Catch & Limitations

items: Model-Specific Derivations: While this works beautifully for Black-Scholes, extending it to more complex models (like Heston or rough fractional Stein-Stein) requires deriving the analytical asymptotic limits first, which is mathematically brutal.

Gating Discontinuities: If the gating network isn't trained or constrained properly, you can get sharp discontinuities at the boundaries between regimes, which can mess up your Greeks (hedging sensitivities).
Implementation Overhead: Writing and maintaining a hybrid system of gating networks, local experts, and high-order numerical solvers is significantly more complex than a standard C++ root-finder.

sections.title: One Article or Paper Worth Reading: LLM Investing Strategies

content.text: The Paper: Can LLM-based Financial Investing Strategies Outperform the Market in Long Run?

If you’ve spent any time looking at financial tech research lately, you’ve probably seen some breathless claims about "AI agents" acting as autonomous portfolio managers and beating the market. Most of these papers are, frankly, full of holes—evaluating their models on tiny, cherry-picked timeframes (like a single year in a roaring bull market) or completely ignoring survivorship bias. This paper, published for the KDD 2026 conference by researchers from Oxford, Edinburgh, and SKKU, is the cold shower the industry desperately needed.
Why This One?

Instead of letting these hyped-up LLM strategies grade their own homework, the authors built a rigorous, bias-aware backtesting framework called FINSABER. They took several highly cited LLM-based trading agents (such as FinMem and FinAgent) and ran them through a brutal 24-year stress test from 2000 to 2024. This period covers the Dot-Com crash, the 2008 Global Financial Crisis, and the COVID-19 shock. They also built in proper real-world controls: including delisted stocks to kill survivorship bias, accounting for transaction costs, and tracking the actual API inference costs of running the models.
The Detailed Summary

The results were a proper pasting for the AI hype. When evaluated over the long run and across a realistic cross-section of over 100 stocks, the supposed "LLM alpha" completely evaporated. But the real kicker isn't just that they underperformed; it's how they underperformed.

In bull markets, the LLM agents proved to be overly conservative, frequently sitting on cash or hedging when they should have been riding the trend, causing them to lag passive benchmarks. In bear markets, they did the exact opposite: they became overly aggressive, catching falling knives and suffering catastrophic drawdowns. Essentially, the models exhibited "wrong-way risk"—the exact opposite of what you want from an active manager.
Key Takeaways

items: The Alpha is an Illusion: Over a multi-decade horizon, LLM-based timing strategies fail to beat simple buy-and-hold benchmarks once you expand the stock universe and account for realistic trading conditions.
Regime-Blindness: LLMs lack a native understanding of market regimes. They get timid during bull runs and recklessly aggressive during market crashes.
Inference Costs Eat the Lunch: Factoring in the actual cost of querying GPT-4 or Claude thousands of times to make daily trading decisions makes the net returns of these strategies look even worse.

The Bias Trap: Most academic papers claiming LLM trading success are heavily contaminated by survivorship bias (ignoring delisted stocks) and look-ahead bias (using future data to make past decisions).

content.text: The Killer Quote

"Our market regime analysis further demonstrates that LLM strategies are overly conservative in bull markets, underperforming passive benchmarks, and overly aggressive in bear markets, incurring heavy losses."
What to Skim vs. What to Read

You can safely skim the heavy mathematical formulations of the reinforcement learning baselines and the exact API schema setups in the appendix. Instead, focus your attention on Section 4 (the empirical results and the regime analysis) and Section 5, which discusses why LLMs fail to adapt to shifting market environments.
Our Take

LLMs are incredible at synthesising unstructured data—summarising 10-Ks, parsing earnings calls, and extracting sentiment. But treating them as end-to-end decision-makers for market timing is a category error. They don't have a native concept of risk-reward or market regimes; they are just predicting the next token based on historical text. If you want to use AI in your investment process, use LLMs as feature extractors, and leave the portfolio construction to traditional quantitative models.

sections.title: People / Business Psychology Idea: The Illusory Truth Effect

content.text: The Illusory Truth Effect: Why Your Brain Loves a Repeated Lie

We like to think of ourselves as highly analytical, rational operators. We build complex multi-tab LBO models, write Python scripts to backtest quantitative strategies, and debate the finer points of the yield curve over a pint of Neck Oil. But under the hood, our brains are incredibly lazy.

When forced to decide if a statement is true, the brain doesn't always go digging through its database of facts. Instead, it checks for something called 'cognitive fluency'—essentially, how easy the information is to process. And the easiest way to make something easy to process? Repeat it.

This is the Illusory Truth Effect (first identified in a 1977 study by Hasher, Goldstein, and Toppino). If you hear a claim repeated often enough, your brain starts to flag it as 'familiar.' And because your brain lazily conflates familiarity with accuracy, you start to believe it’s true—even if you initially knew it was complete rubbish. In fact, a famous 2015 study by Lisa Fazio and colleagues proved that prior knowledge doesn't protect you from this; even if you know a fact is wrong, repeating the lie still makes you more likely to believe it.

Think of the classic market narratives that get repeated so often they become gospel. Remember when WeWork was 'a technology platform, not a real estate company'? Or the endless repetition of 'AI will replace junior analysts by next Tuesday'? In the corporate world, this happens on a smaller scale every day. A project manager slides a bullet point into a deck: 'Project Apollo will deliver 40% efficiency gains.' It’s a finger-in-the-wind estimate. But after three months of weekly standups where that slide is shown, the entire department—including the CFO—is treating that 40% figure as an immutable law of physics.
How to use it

items: The Audit: When reviewing a pitch, a stock thesis, or an internal proposal, highlight the 'obvious' assumptions. Ask yourself: Do I actually have primary data for this, or have I just read it on Bloomberg and Slack twenty times this week?

The Pitch: If you’re selling a deal, pitching a fund, or interviewing for a new role, pick one clear, simple anchor narrative and repeat it. Don't overcomplicate it. If you want them to think of you as 'the structured credit specialist,' weave that phrase into your introduction, your deal walkthrough, and your closing remarks. By the time they debrief, their brains will have accepted it as a hard fact.

content.text: One line to remember: If you hear a market narrative thirty times, it’s probably not a trend—it’s a trap.
